question: How many cases are there in all, counting those no list caught?

mony2015.cite: Mony, Varghese & Thomas (2015). Estimation of perinatal mortality rate for institutional births in Rajasthan state, India, using capture–recapture technique. BMJ Open 5: e005966.

steps.title: Two lists
steps.text: Take two (or more) sources that each record some of the cases, such as hospital registers and a community follow-up. Neither needs to be complete.

quotes.text: This method is based on matching two or more independent samples to arrive at an estimate of the total number of diseases/events when both of the lists are potentially incomplete but with a definite overlap.

steps.title: Match
steps.text: Find the cases that appear on both lists. With no shared ID number, match on several details at once. In ecology the tag on an animal does this job.

quotes.text: In its most classical form an estimate of the size of a species’ population is calculated after capturing, tagging and recapturing animals.
If an identifying variable can be recorded on a list at every capture occasion, tagging is unnecessary. The capture-recapture histories become apparent by merging the lists.

steps.title: Count the overlap
steps.text: Sort every case into: list A only, list B only, both. In the Rajasthan study, 12, 20 and 21 early neonatal deaths, 53 in all.

steps.title: Estimate the total
steps.text: If the lists are independent, the share of list B that list A also found estimates how much of everything list A found. The paper's form: N = (A+1)(B+1)/(both+1) − 1.

quotes.text: The Lincoln-Petersen unbiased formula was used to estimate the true number of perinatal deaths
The total number of estimated early neonatal deaths worked out to a total of 64 by the CR method (with 11 being missed by both).

steps.title: Check the assumptions
steps.text: The estimate rests on a closed population, reliable matching, independent lists and equal chances of being caught. Lists that catch the same people push the estimate down.

quotes.text: The validity of the estimates relies on four key assumptions: (1) the population being studied must be ‘closed’, (2) individuals must be matched reliably, (3) sources should be independent and (4) the chance of being ‘captured’ by a source must be equal.
As the dependence between sources increases, the bias of the Lincoln-Petersen estimator and the Chapman estimator, will increase

exercise.title: Count what no list saw
exercise.intro: First the published counts from Rajasthan, then a population whose true size you know, caught by two lists.

quote.text: Capture–recapture methods allow for the estimation of an unknown population size by using two or more samples from that population.

real.label: Early neonatal deaths, Rajasthan (Mony et al. 2015, Results)

exercise.data_label: The first part uses the published counts. The population in the second part is example data, made up and drawn with a fixed seed; each dot is a person: amber caught by list A only, blue by list B only, filled by both, empty by neither.
